screens.title: What is a Write Operation?
screens.narratorSegment: A write operation is any contract call that changes blockchain state. Unlike view or pure calls, which only read state, write operations require a transaction: the caller must sign the transaction, include it in the network, and miners will include it in a block. Because changes consume computational resources, the EVM charges gas which the sender pays. Concretely, in SimpleStorage calling setData(42) requires encoding the function call into the transaction's data field and paying gas for execution. An important practical point: even if a transaction reverts because of a failed require, the gas used until the revert is still consumed. A common misconception is that reverts return state to a previous snapshot and refund gas — reverts do undo state changes but they do not refund gas already consumed. A short example: you prepare the txObject, use contract. methods. setData(42). encodeABI() for data, sign the tx, then send it. If the receipt. status is true you can safely query getData again to observe the new value; if false, the stored value remains unchanged. Reflect on this: when would you optimistically update your UI before a receipt, and what checks would you need to avoid showing incorrect state?

content.html:
Core Concept What is a Write Operation?

What is a Write Operation?

A precise definition and a real example using SimpleStorage.setData.

Definition & mechanics
  • • Write operations require a signed transaction that is mined into a block.
  • • The transaction carries encoded function data created by encodeABI.
  • • Execution consumes gas; reverts still consume gas used until failure.
Concrete example
Calling SimpleStorage.setData(42), signing the tx, and reading getData after receipt.status confirms success.
Key Takeaway
Only update UI after a confirmed receipt; reverts do not change state but consume gas.
Common misconception

A revert does not restore gas or free the user from cost. The EVM undoes state changes, but the gas used to reach that point is paid. Treat a false receipt.status as a full failure and re-query state before assuming anything changed.

Check your understanding
Why is it unsafe to optimistically show the new stored value before the transaction is confirmed?
Analogy
Think of the receipt as a bank confirmation: until you get it you can't assume money moved.

screens.title: Transaction lifecycle for a contract write
screens.narratorSegment: A write transaction follows a clear lifecycle you must manage. First, instantiate the contract with its ABI and address. Then prepare the transaction object with fields: from (sender), to (contract address), data (encoded function call), optional value for payable calls, gasPrice, gasLimit, and nonce. Next, estimate gas on the specific contract method; add a small buffer to make gasLimit slightly higher than the estimate. After that sign the transaction — either by signing locally with a private key or by triggering the wallet to sign — and then broadcast using sendSignedTransaction or eth_sendTransaction via a wallet. When the node returns a receipt, check receipt. status, receipt. transactionHash, and gasUsed. If status is true, re-query contract state to reflect the change. If status is false or an exception occurred, inspect error messages for revert hints like a require failure. A common misconception is to reuse a generic gas estimate for all methods; instead always estimate on the exact method and parameters. Given this flow, how would you surface confirmation status to a user to avoid confusion about finality? Transaction lifecycle for a contract write means build tx object, estimate gas, sign, send, read receipt, then re-query state and inform the user based on receipt.status.. In practical terms, from building the tx object to confirmation and re-query. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Process Flow Transaction lifecycle

Transaction lifecycle for a contract write

Step-by-step actions needed to execute and confirm a write.

1
Instantiate contract
Use new web3.eth.Contract(abi, address) to create a contract instance you can call methods on.
2
Prepare txObject
  • • from, to, data (encodeABI), optional value, gasPrice, gasLimit, nonce
3
Estimate, sign, send
Call method.estimateGas, sign with private key or wallet, then sendSignedTransaction or let wallet handle signing and broadcasting.
Confirmations & receipts
When a receipt is returned, check receipt.status. If true, query the contract again to read updated state. If false, treat it as a revert: state unchanged, gas spent.

Estimate gas for setData(42), add 10% buffer, sign and send, then verify receipt.status is true before reading getData.
Common mistake
Re-using a single gasLimit for different methods — always estimate per-method and per-parameter set.
Key Takeaway

Follow the lifecycle strictly: build, estimate, sign, send, check receipt, then refresh state.

keyIdea.text: Fetch nonce and gas, encode the contract method, sign the transaction, then broadcast and read the returned receipt to determine success.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough Signing & sending

Signing and sending a transaction

Terminal-style script that signs locally and broadcasts a transaction to Ganache.

Core code excerpt
const Web3 = require('web3');
const web3 = new Web3('http://127.0.0.1:7545');

const simpleStorageABI = [ /* ... ABI ... */ ];
const simpleStorageAddress = '0x...';

async function writeToContract() {
  const simpleStorage = new web3.eth.Contract(simpleStorageABI, simpleStorageAddress);
  const accounts = await web3.eth.getAccounts();
  const senderAddress = accounts[0];
  const senderPrivateKey = '0x...';

  const initialData = await simpleStorage.methods.getData().call();
  const newData = 42;
  const nonce = await web3.eth.getTransactionCount(senderAddress, 'pending');
  const estimatedGas = await simpleStorage.methods.setData(newData).estimateGas({ from: senderAddress });
  const gasLimit = Math.round(estimatedGas * 1.1);
  const gasPrice = await web3.eth.getGasPrice();

  const txObject = {
    from: senderAddress,
    to: simpleStorageAddress,
    data: simpleStorage.methods.setData(newData).encodeABI(),
    gasPrice: gasPrice,
    gasLimit: gasLimit,
    nonce: nonce,
  };

  const signedTx = await web3.eth.accounts.signTransaction(txObject, senderPrivateKey);
  const receipt = await web3.eth.sendSignedTransaction(signedTx.rawTransaction);
  console.log('Status:', receipt.status);
}

writeToContract();
Explanation bullets
  • • Use getTransactionCount(sender, 'pending') to calculate nonce when multiple transactions may be pending.
  • • estimateGas on the method gives a tailored gas figure for that call and parameters.
  • • Always sign with the correct private key; placeholders will cause the script to abort.
Concrete example
Run with newData = 42 to succeed, then set newData = 1500 to trigger a require(_data < 1000) and observe a revert.
Pro tip

Log nonce and gas values during development to verify they match expectations before broadcasting.

screens.title: Payable function calls vs direct Ether transfers
screens.narratorSegment: Payable functions allow a contract to receive Ether as part of the function execution. Calling a payable function requires including a value field in the txObject or send() call. A direct Ether transfer sends Ether to an address without invoking a contract function. The practical difference matters: if a function requires a specific value or is not marked payable, sending value incorrectly will cause a revert. For example, if a deposit() function is payable and you send 0.5 ETH, the contract can accept and process that value. If deposit() were not payable and you attempted the same call with value, the EVM would revert and the receipt. status would be false. Developers sometimes mistakenly treat payable as optional — in fact, without the payable modifier Solidity prevents receiving Ether and will revert. When building a dApp, always check the function’s payable annotation and estimate gas including the value parameter. For user experience, show the expected Ether amount, require explicit confirmation, and on revert explain that the contract rejected the value. Ask yourself: how will you surface the revert reason so the user can correct the input amount?

keyIdea.title: Payable vs transfer
keyIdea.text: Only payable functions accept Ether in the same transaction; sending value to a non-payable function causes a revert and consumes gas.

content.html:
Comparison Payable vs direct transfer

Payable function calls vs direct Ether transfers

Understand the behavioral and safety differences for including value in contract calls.

Payable function
  • • Marked payable in Solidity to accept Ether with execution.
  • • Include value in send or txObject when calling the method.
  • • Example: myContract.methods.deposit().send({ from, value: web3.utils.toWei('0.5','ether') })
Direct Ether transfer
  • • Sends Ether to an address without invoking a contract function logic path.
  • • If the recipient is a contract, its fallback/receive function runs; if absent or not payable to accept value as expected, the transfer may fail.
  • • Always confirm the contract's intended acceptance pattern before sending value.
If you send value to a non-payable function, the transaction reverts and gas is consumed.
Design the UX to ask for explicit confirmation of amounts and display revert reasons when possible.

screens.title: Using encodeABI and estimateGas
screens.narratorSegment: Two essential Web3. js primitives for writes are contract. methods. yourFunction(params). encodeABI() and contract. methods. yourFunction(params). estimateGas(options). encodeABI serializes the function selector and parameters into the data field of a transaction so the EVM knows which function and arguments to execute. Without correct encoding, the contract will not identify the call and will likely revert. estimateGas simulates execution on the node and returns the gas units a call will consume under current state, given the caller and parameters. This per-method estimate is crucial because different functions and inputs consume widely different gas. A common misconception is to copy a flat gasLimit across all contract calls; this risks both out-of-gas errors and paying unnecessarily high costs. In practice you call estimateGas with the same from and value parameters as the final transaction, then multiply by a small buffer (for example, 1.1) to set gasLimit. Example: const estimatedGas = await contract. methods. setData(42). estimateGas({ from: sender }); const gasLimit = Math. round(estimatedGas * 1.1); Why would you still sometimes override estimateGas with a higher manual limit in production, and what trade-offs does that introduce?

content.html:
Definition encodeABI & estimateGas

Using encodeABI and estimateGas

How encodeABI and estimateGas work together to create reliable tx objects.

encodeABI

Serializes the method selector and parameters into a data hex string. This is required for the EVM to invoke the intended function.

Example: contract.methods.setData(42).encodeABI() used as txObject.data.
estimateGas

Simulates the transaction on the node using current contract state and returns gas units required. Provide the same from and value options you will send.

Tip: multiply estimate by a small buffer, such as 1.1, to compute gasLimit.
Key Takeaway

Always encode the method call and estimate gas for that exact method and parameters to avoid incorrect execution or wasted gas.

Common-mistake
Using a default gasLimit copied from elsewhere rather than per-method estimation, which can cause failures or overspending.

screens.title: Transaction receipts, confirmations, and status
screens.narratorSegment: A transaction receipt is the canonical record that tells you whether a write succeeded and what resources it consumed. In Web3. js v1. x, receipt. status is a boolean: true indicates success, false indicates a revert. Receipts also include transactionHash, blockNumber, gasUsed, and logs. After you receive a receipt with status true, you should re-query relevant contract state to reflect the change in your UI or backend. If receipt. status is false, the contract execution reverted — state changes were undone, but the gas used until the revert was charged. A frequent misunderstanding is assuming a returned error will always contain a human-readable revert reason. Some nodes or network configurations strip or omit revert messages; you may need to capture errors thrown by sendSignedTransaction or check logs to diagnose issues. Example: after sending a signed tx, check receipt. transactionHash and then call contract. methods. getData(). call() only on success. For dApps, consider showing the transaction hash and guidance when status is false so users can inspect the failure. What information will you prioritize in a failure message to help a user recover?

content.html:
Definition Receipts & confirmations

Transaction receipts, confirmations, and status

What to read from a receipt and how to use it to update your dApp.

Receipt fields to use
  • • transactionHash: uniquely identifies the transaction on-chain.
  • • blockNumber: shows the block that included the transaction.
  • • gasUsed: gas actually consumed by the transaction.
  • • status: true or false indicating success or revert.

Assuming status false will always include a readable revert reason — sometimes it will not, and additional debugging is needed.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity Successful write & revert

Demonstrating a successful write and a revert

Step-by-step tasks to run on Ganache and observe both outcomes.

Steps
  1. Deploy modified SimpleStorage with require(_data < 1000) in setData.
  2. Update ABI and address in writeToContract script; set senderPrivateKey from Ganache.
  3. Run with newData = 42; confirm receipt.status true and getData shows 42.
  4. Run with newData = 1500; observe revert, receipt.status false or thrown error, and getData unchanged.
Tips & checks
  • • Verify private key is correct; placeholders halt the script.
  • • Use nonce = getTransactionCount(sender, 'pending') to prevent collisions.
  • • Capture gasUsed from receipt to show cost even on revert.
Key Takeaway

Reproducing both success and revert scenarios is the fastest way to learn how to respond correctly in your dApp and to craft helpful user messages.

screens.title: Error handling, retries, and UX for reverts
screens.narratorSegment: Robust error handling is essential for a good user experience. Wrap sendSignedTransaction calls in try/catch and log errors. Inspect error. message for common clues such as 'reverted', 'insufficient funds', or 'nonce too low'. When a revert occurs, provide users with a clear message that the transaction failed and that gas was consumed; avoid implying the state changed. For network issues or temporary failures, implement a retry policy only when safe: retries are appropriate for transient network errors but not for transactions that already appear mined. For dApps that use wallets, rely on window. ethereum. request for user signing and handle user rejection separately from network or contract errors. Keep users informed with transaction hashes so they can inspect the chain if desired. A misconception to avoid is automatically retrying a transaction without checking its on-chain status — you may double-spend or cause nonce conflicts. Instead, query the node for the transaction hash before retrying or increment the nonce intentionally. What feedback would you display in the UI to distinguish a user-rejected signature from a contract revert? Error handling, retries, and UX for reverts means catch errors, diagnose revert reasons, avoid blind retries, and show clear user-facing messages including txhash and cause when available.. Best Practices Error handling & UX

Error handling, retries, and UX for reverts

Patterns to diagnose failures and keep users informed without introducing risk.

Developer checklist
  • • Wrap sendSignedTransaction in try/catch and log error.message.
  • • Check for 'reverted', 'insufficient funds', 'nonce too low' in messages.
  • • On revert, re-query contract state instead of assuming change.
UX guidance
  • • Show transaction hash immediately so users can track progress.
  • • Distinguish signature rejection from network errors and contract reverts.
  • • Never optimistically show success; wait for receipt.status true.
Common mistake

Automatically retrying a transaction without checking its on-chain status can cause duplicate effects or nonce clashes. Design retries with care and always confirm the txHash first.

fullNarratorScript:
Write operations are the way a smart contract actually changes the blockchain. In this chapter you will learn what makes a write operation different from a read, why signed transactions and gas are required, and how Web3. js turns a function call into a transaction the EVM can execute. We’ll use the SimpleStorage example to show a successful setData call, then intentionally trigger a require condition to observe a revert and learn how to diagnose it. You will also learn how to include Ether when calling payable functions and how to interpret a transaction receipt’s status field. These skills matter because every state change costs gas and can fail; your dApp must prepare accurate gas estimates, manage nonces, and handle errors gracefully to give users correct feedback. As you follow the examples, notice how encodeABI creates the data payload, estimateGas predicts cost, and sendSignedTransaction delivers a final receipt. By the end, you should be confident constructing a transaction object, signing it, and responding correctly to both success and revert outcomes. What would you show a user first when a write operation fails?

By the end of this lesson you will be able to construct and send transactions that invoke state-changing functions on a smart contract, estimate gas and set transaction parameters, handle receipts and confirmations to validate the outcome, and distinguish sending Ether directly from invoking payable contract functions. Each objective is a practical skill: building the transaction object requires a correct ABI and encoded data; estimating gas prevents out-of-gas failures; interpreting receipt. status ensures your dApp does not assume success; and handling payable logic prevents accidental reverts when value is wrong. For example, you will practice calling SimpleStorage. setData so you can see nonce calculation, estimateGas, and a final receipt with status true. You will also intentionally cause a revert by sending a value that violates a require condition to learn how error messages clue you into contract logic issues. Understanding these objectives helps you design safer dApps that surface clear feedback to users and recover gracefully when writes fail. Which of these skills would you test first in your development workflow?

This second objectives slide links each skill to the hands-on steps you will perform. First, constructing and sending transactions maps to creating the txObject with contract. methods. setData. encodeABI(), adding from and to addresses, and including a value when calling payable methods. Second, estimating gas translates to calling method. estimateGas and adding a buffer to prevent out-of-gas failures. Third, handling receipts ties to reading receipt. transactionHash, receipt. gasUsed, and receipt. status to decide whether to refresh contract state. Fourth, differentiating transfers is practiced by calling a payable deposit function with value and observing that sending value to a non-payable function will revert. Each practice item is aimed at building confidence with real Ganache accounts, nonces, and private-key signing. A common misconception is that a reverted transaction returns state — it does not; only the gas is lost. As you practice, ask: what user feedback will clearly show gas consumption vs. a state change? This helps you design both robust code and a clear UI for your users.

A write operation is any contract call that changes blockchain state. Unlike view or pure calls, which only read state, write operations require a transaction: the caller must sign the transaction, include it in the network, and miners will include it in a block. Because changes consume computational resources, the EVM charges gas which the sender pays. Concretely, in SimpleStorage calling setData(42) requires encoding the function call into the transaction's data field and paying gas for execution. An important practical point: even if a transaction reverts because of a failed require, the gas used until the revert is still consumed. A common misconception is that reverts return state to a previous snapshot and refund gas — reverts do undo state changes but they do not refund gas already consumed. A short example: you prepare the txObject, use contract. methods. setData(42). encodeABI() for data, sign the tx, then send it. If the receipt. status is true you can safely query getData again to observe the new value; if false, the stored value remains unchanged. Reflect on this: when would you optimistically update your UI before a receipt, and what checks would you need to avoid showing incorrect state?

A write transaction follows a clear lifecycle you must manage. First, instantiate the contract with its ABI and address. Then prepare the transaction object with fields: from (sender), to (contract address), data (encoded function call), optional value for payable calls, gasPrice, gasLimit, and nonce. Next, estimate gas on the specific contract method; add a small buffer to make gasLimit slightly higher than the estimate. After that sign the transaction — either by signing locally with a private key or by triggering the wallet to sign — and then broadcast using sendSignedTransaction or eth_sendTransaction via a wallet. When the node returns a receipt, check receipt. status, receipt. transactionHash, and gasUsed. If status is true, re-query contract state to reflect the change. If status is false or an exception occurred, inspect error messages for revert hints like a require failure. A common misconception is to reuse a generic gas estimate for all methods; instead always estimate on the exact method and parameters. Given this flow, how would you surface confirmation status to a user to avoid confusion about finality? Transaction lifecycle for a contract write means build tx object, estimate gas, sign, send, read receipt, then re-query state and inform the user based on receipt.status.. In practical terms, from building the tx object to confirmation and re-query. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through the example script that performs a write to SimpleStorage. The script connects to a local Ganache node, instantiates the contract with ABI and address, and selects a sender account. Key steps: it reads the current value via getData to show pre-state, prepares newData, fetches the nonce with getTransactionCount, calls estimateGas on setData to get an accurate gas estimate, computes a gasLimit buffer, obtains a gasPrice, builds txObject with encodeABI in data, signs the transaction with a private key, and finally sends the signed transaction using web3. eth. sendSignedTransaction. After the transaction is mined, the receipt gives transactionHash, blockNumber, gasUsed, and status. A typical mistake is leaving placeholder private keys or contract addresses in the script — this will immediately stop execution. Another is forgetting to use the 'pending' flag when getting the nonce in environments with multiple in-flight transactions. In practice, run the script first with a valid newData like 42 to see success, then change newData to a value that violates your contract's require statement to produce a revert. How will you log and display the revert reason in your dApp to help users recover?

Payable functions allow a contract to receive Ether as part of the function execution. Calling a payable function requires including a value field in the txObject or send() call. A direct Ether transfer sends Ether to an address without invoking a contract function. The practical difference matters: if a function requires a specific value or is not marked payable, sending value incorrectly will cause a revert. For example, if a deposit() function is payable and you send 0.5 ETH, the contract can accept and process that value. If deposit() were not payable and you attempted the same call with value, the EVM would revert and the receipt. status would be false. Developers sometimes mistakenly treat payable as optional — in fact, without the payable modifier Solidity prevents receiving Ether and will revert. When building a dApp, always check the function’s payable annotation and estimate gas including the value parameter. For user experience, show the expected Ether amount, require explicit confirmation, and on revert explain that the contract rejected the value. Ask yourself: how will you surface the revert reason so the user can correct the input amount?

Two essential Web3. js primitives for writes are contract. methods. yourFunction(params). encodeABI() and contract. methods. yourFunction(params). estimateGas(options). encodeABI serializes the function selector and parameters into the data field of a transaction so the EVM knows which function and arguments to execute. Without correct encoding, the contract will not identify the call and will likely revert. estimateGas simulates execution on the node and returns the gas units a call will consume under current state, given the caller and parameters. This per-method estimate is crucial because different functions and inputs consume widely different gas. A common misconception is to copy a flat gasLimit across all contract calls; this risks both out-of-gas errors and paying unnecessarily high costs. In practice you call estimateGas with the same from and value parameters as the final transaction, then multiply by a small buffer (for example, 1.1) to set gasLimit. Example: const estimatedGas = await contract. methods. setData(42). estimateGas({ from: sender }); const gasLimit = Math. round(estimatedGas * 1.1); Why would you still sometimes override estimateGas with a higher manual limit in production, and what trade-offs does that introduce?

A transaction receipt is the canonical record that tells you whether a write succeeded and what resources it consumed. In Web3. js v1. x, receipt. status is a boolean: true indicates success, false indicates a revert. Receipts also include transactionHash, blockNumber, gasUsed, and logs. After you receive a receipt with status true, you should re-query relevant contract state to reflect the change in your UI or backend. If receipt. status is false, the contract execution reverted — state changes were undone, but the gas used until the revert was charged. A frequent misunderstanding is assuming a returned error will always contain a human-readable revert reason. Some nodes or network configurations strip or omit revert messages; you may need to capture errors thrown by sendSignedTransaction or check logs to diagnose issues. Example: after sending a signed tx, check receipt. transactionHash and then call contract. methods. getData(). call() only on success. For dApps, consider showing the transaction hash and guidance when status is false so users can inspect the failure. What information will you prioritize in a failure message to help a user recover?
